title: Roke agitated before discharge
article: The day before Matt Roke was discharged from the Elmgrove psychiatric centre - and months prior to being fatally shot by provincial police during a psychotic episode - the man acted belligerently towards staff and fellow patients.

Roke cursed workers, threw a candy at one staff member and shut a door on the finger of another patient on Feb. 27 that year, according to reports from Elmgrove at the time, read into the record Tuesday by lead counsel John Semenoff at the inquest into the man's shooting death.
The actions did not dissuade attending psychiatrist Dr. Jeffrey Jackson's decision the next day to discharge the Maitland resident after a turbulent month-long stay.
On four occasions, including when he was brought in for assessment, Roke was listed as an involuntary patient after he abused privileges.
But on the day before his discharge, Roke's aggressive behaviour resulted from him being intoxicated, said Jackson.
It is unclear how he got the booze, but it was part of a pattern. Roke had gone off the grounds several times to seek alcohol, one of his co-addictions along with nicotine that Jackson identified.
Jackson acknowledged to the inquest Roke's violent behaviour was out of character with his past mental health crises.
Roke assaulted a store clerk on Jan. 31 that resulted in his being apprehended by police and ultimately taken for assessment at Elmgrove.
While on a pass, Roke also grabbed his father's hair after his request for money to buy booze was refused.

But Jackson insisted there were good reasons for the discharge. Roke, for example, had taken his medication for two weeks and his symptoms such as incoherent thoughts and delusions were under control. Secondly, he had found a place to live, with an uncle in Dundas County.
Jackson didn't know of misgivings expressed by Roke's parents about the living arrangements.

Roke refused to consider living in a group home setting provided by Leeds and Grenville Mental Health, which the doctor felt would be ideal. But living with his uncle was a better option than having Roke on his own, considering his frequent and often negligent smoking habit was a fire hazard, said Jackson.
Roke also had a penchant for being active at night and often disturbed neighbours when he lived in apartments, the inquest has heard.

Jackson met the uncle, who was advised to remove any access to alcohol from his home, and while he didn't have serious reservations about the new arrangements, he did report some concerns in his notes.
"The prognosis in his case was guarded. The outcome was not likely to be successful because he wouldn't allow us to put the supports in place," said Jackson.
It is common for men of Roke's age with schizophrenia to be in and out of the mental health care system unless they have proper supports.

Jackson hoped Roke, 33, would eventually take advantage of services available to him, though the doctor said he was not in the role of ensuring that took place while he focussed his attention on caring for active Elmgrove patients.

Asked for suggestions to improve the system the five-member inquest jury could consider, Jackson said informal weekly meetings held to discuss patients' needs with a range of health care professionals should be better recorded to avoid loose ends.
He agreed with a suggestion that meetings should involve the patients and their loved ones when cases are being discussed.

The attending psychiatrist to Matthew Roke at the former Elmgrove acute-care centre lamented the slow pace of change in how mental illness is perceived during an inquest Tuesday into the fatal provincial police shooting of the patient in May, 2012.
Dr. Jeffrey Jackson said Roke has been incorrectly identified as a schizophrenic, a label which stigmatizes the 33-year-old Maitland man.
Instead, Roke was a man who suffered paranoid schizophrenia and should be identified that way, just like people with other diseases such as a person with cancer, said Jackson.
"He had a physical illness of the brain," said the doctor.
